clips.title: Pacing
clips.listenFor: Pauses on meaning, not commas: the four-comma clause stays one unit; the biggest pause is before "and isn't", which has no punctuation.
clips.text: Before you move the backups, check two things. First, whether the new drive has room — it needs about forty gigabytes, which, if you've kept the old photo library, it probably doesn't. Second, that none of your connected accounts (calendar, email, and the shared drive from last spring) is still syncing, because a copy made mid-sync looks complete and isn't.

clips.title: Code-switching, whole phrases
clips.listenFor: Accent and prosody at each switch into Spanish, German, and French; the name Lucía.
clips.text: Lucía said, and I quote, "el martes es imposible." Klaus just replied "na ja, Donnerstag geht auch." Et la réservation ? C'est déjà fait.
clips.pronounce: Lucía is loo-SEE-ah. Spanish “el martes es imposible” (“Tuesday is impossible”): el MAR-tess ess eem-po-SEE-bleh. German “na ja, Donnerstag geht auch” (“oh well, Thursday works too”): NAH-yah, a shrug, often run together as one word; then DON-ers-tahk gate OWKH, the final ch a breathy sound as in Scottish “loch”. French “Et la réservation ? C'est déjà fait.” (“And the reservation? It's already done.”): ay lah ray-zair-vah-SYOHN? say day-ZHAH FEH.

clips.title: Single German words
clips.listenFor: Schnapsidee and Stammtisch said as German words inside an English sentence, without the rest going German.
clips.text: It was really a Schnapsidee, cooked up at the Stammtisch.
clips.pronounce: Schnapsidee (a harebrained idea; literally a schnapps idea): SHNAHPS-ee-day. Stammtisch (the regulars' table at a pub): SHTAHM-tish. In both, the opening s sounds like sh.
